So General Tolimir will be able to follow along with the actual video. So they -- it's been subtitled into English for our purposes, but the original is in B/C/S. So I think we should be okay for the remainder of the video presentations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon again to you and Your Honours. Now, where I left off was beginning to discuss the assistant commanders of General Mladic. We spoke about the staff sector which was headed by the Chief of Staff, and technically speaking General Milovanovic was not an assistant commander in the same way that General Tolimir was an assistant commander. He was the Chief of Staff. He was the first among equals. He had this inherent power to issue combat orders which absent specific delegated authority from General Mladic the other assistant commanders did not. But the evidence we will see will show that, in fact, the assistant commanders were empowered to issue combat orders on occasion if they had that authority delegated to them. Let me spend just a couple of minutes describing generally what the role of the assistant commanders was in the Main Staff. You may have heard me refer to professional line of command or professional chain of command. What that refers to is in the Main Staff, similar to any almost corporation, you had different sections that had different specialties. So we had security and intelligence, logistics, morale, and each of these sectors in the Main Staff was headed by an assistant commander, and sometimes we refer to this as the professional line, sometimes we refer to it as the specialist line, sometimes we refer to it as the expert line, but they all basically mean the same thing. An assistant commander is an assistant commander for a certain expertise or area, intelligence and security, rear services, morale, personnel, and so forth. And they each reported directly to General Mladic. And within each of these sectors, the assistant commander had officers that he himself directly commanded in a professional sense and to whom he could issue orders that fell within a particular professional line, as it were. So these were -- and we'll talk about some specifics in a minute, but these were branches that all reported through the assistant commanders, like General Tolimir, directly to Mladic but had their own areas of expertise. And we'll see how they operated together as a unit in a little bit. Now, it was the job of each of these assistant commanders to make proposals to General Mladic within their specific field of expertise, be it logistics, be it the morale of the army, be it intelligence and security matters. So their job was to make these proposals which Mladic would consider and either adopt, reject, or modify, and ultimately make a decision. And if General Mladic did issue an order based on an assistant commanders's proposal, it was then the assistant commander's obligation to make sure that General Mladic's order was fulfilled and implemented on the ground, all the way down the line. And the assistant commander would do that by professionally controlling, as we refer to it, by directing, as we also refer to it, expertly managing, as we sometimes refer to it, the officers who fell underneath that professional line. And it was their obligation to make sure that the job got done according to their understood intent of General Mladic. They knew what General Mladic wanted and they would make sure that their men did what had to be done to get that accomplished on the ground. Now, in addition to being able to issue orders within their own field of expertise, for example, General Djukic, the head of rear services could tell somebody to go transfer this amount of boots somewhere else, the assistant commander was held responsible himself to General Mladic for the work that that assistant commander's subordinates were doing or weren't doing in the field. So the assistant commander is always accountable, as it were, for the work done by his professional subordinates. That's why you had that assistant commander there, to manage those specialist branches down the line. So let's look -- spend a couple of minutes, please, looking at some of the individual assistant commanders and their sectors and talk about what they do. The first one I want to talk about is General Gvero's morale sector. And we see here that his title is assistant commander for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs. And by moral guidance, that incorporates a number of concepts, but the most important one was combat morale, that is making sure that the fighters in the trenches have the will to continue to fight, that they understand what the fight is about, that they're going to retain their respect for command and do what they're told. And it was General Gvero's job to monitor the state of morale throughout the army, to make sure that that morale wasn't weakening, that soldiers weren't deserting their posts, for example. And you'll see that General Gvero and General Tolimir had to co-operate a fair amount because there was overlap between their two areas. For example, if you have a lot of desertions or crimes being committed within a certain unit, not only is that an indication that you might have a morale problem, but it's an indication that you might have a security problem, and that would be of interest to General Tolimir as well. So you have co-operation and overlap going on. Same thing with respect to propaganda and psychological activities. Because it was General Tolimir's job to make an assessment of the enemy's forces and intentions, that meant knowing what your enemy was up to and that meant trying to get inside your enemy's head, and that necessarily involved propaganda and counter-propaganda, and psychological operations. So we'll see overlap in that area as well. And we have here on the screen Lieutenant-Colonel Milovan Milutinovic. He was chief of the department for information and psychological propaganda activities. He headed up the Main Staff's information centre, and he reported to General Gvero. You'll see Colonel Milutinovic on the ground. You'll see him at the Hotel Fontana meetings you've probably heard about. You'll see him in Zepa. You'll see General Tolimir issue an order for loud-speakers to be brought to Zepa for Colonel Milutinovic for the purpose of broadcasting propaganda messages to the Zepa civilians that, "You can't stay any longer in Zepa." This was a common tactic used by the VRS. General Gvero was also responsible for legal affairs, which meant monitoring what was happening with respect to disciplinary matters, criminal matters. There was a whole separate process through the military court system that handled that, but it was General Gvero's responsibility to have oversight over that. Again, because if you have a suddenly high number of criminal acts being committed, violence, soldier-on-soldier violence in a unit, that can be indicative of a morale problem, so General Gvero had his eye on that issue. And given the religious nature of this war, the religious affairs aspect was something that General Gvero was responsible for. That meant liaising with the community, with the religious community, the Serbian Orthodox church basically. And you'll see members of the church involved in various activities, events, celebrations during this trial. Just a quick note. We have the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs. That was headed by General Skrbic, and essentially his sector was responsible for overseeing the mobilisation of people, materiel, as well as the education and assignment of officers. And then we have Djordje Djukic, General Djukic, who was head of rear services, also known as logistics. That sector was responsible, as you can imagine, for procuring, distributing war materiel, the needs of the army, weapons, fuel, clothing, and maintaining the various logistics bases that the army had throughout the war theatre. Now, let's go to the intelligence and security sector. Let me start by just showing you a transcript of an address that General Tolimir made to a particularly contentious RS National Assembly session in 1995. This was in Sanski Most, and some members of the army had come in for some criticism. And I think, as we'll see, General Tolimir described his job obviously pretty well, pretty succinctly. Gathering intelligence about the enemy's strength, plans, and intentions. The organs under his charge have successfully secured information of strategic significance about the political and military leadership, on the basis of which we could obtain accurate assessments about the behaviour of the Serbian enemies and on this basis, and this is what's important, the corresponding decisions. He refers to here his daily intelligence and security reports that he and his staff would compile and send out again to President Karadzic and all the relevant security intelligence bodies in the army and across the river to the VJ. And he says: "Every day I supply this information ... I've sent them since the beginning of the war ..." And you'll see that he takes responsibility. "I am willing to do so for my collaborators who are my understudies when I am absent who process the information ..." He says, I am willing to be dismissed, because he takes responsibility for their work. So basically this intelligence is gathered through a variety of means, informants, captured documents, interrogating POWs, interceptions of radio and telephone communications. And you will also hear that the intelligence administration was responsible for planning and directing reconnaissance actions, which means sending soldiers deep to gather information as well as sabotage. Just briefly, security, on the other hand, versus intelligence entailed three main areas. First, counter-intelligence. It might sound a little odd, but counter-intelligence didn't fall under the intelligence administration; it fell under the security administration. Counter-intelligence is trying to identify and thwart internal enemies, traitors, spies, and denying to the enemy the very kinds of information that you're trying to find out about them. That was what counter-intelligence was about. And with that information the security organs had the obligation to inform their commanders of these threats and to propose ways to counter them. The second area under security was criminal legal duties, such as prosecuting the soldiers for criminal violations and apprehending deserters. Now, it wasn't the security administration that acted as the lawyers, but it was the MPs, for example, the military policemen operating under the security administration who would go out and make the arrests. It would be lawyers usually within an MP or security unit who would be drawing up the initial documents. And third, related to what I just said, the security administration - and this is critical for our case - oversaw the work of the military police units. The duties of the military police included physical protection of key personnel, facilities, traffic control, plus crime prevention activities, like I just mentioned, and, importantly, prisoners of war, escorting, guarding. Now, General Tolimir oversaw both of these administrations, and obviously it makes sense to have one person do that because there's a lot of overlap between the two. Each administration, as you will hear, had its own chief. The chief of the intelligence administration was Petar Salapura, and the chief of the security administration was Ljubisa Beara, and I'll talk about each of those areas in a moment. And as I mentioned before, as the immediate professional superior of Salapura and Beara, General Tolimir could directly issue orders to them and commands within his line of expertise. And he could also pass on orders to them from his own superiors, from General Tolimir's own superiors, like General Mladic or even the president. Of course, if he received an order from the president what he would be duty-bound to do in the first instance was to inform his immediate superior, and that would be Ratko Mladic. In turn, Salapura and Beara were duty-bound to report to General Tolimir and advise him on important developments and make proposals to him and carry out and supervise the implementation of orders that General Tolimir issued or passed on to them. And this was true up and down all the professional lines. That's how it worked. Subordinates were duty-bound to report up to their superiors that they'd accomplished the tasks that they'd been given. Now, General Mladic could directly issue an order to Colonel Beara or Colonel Salapura, but if he did so the first person they would have to inform would be General Tolimir. And that is because he had to know. These were his men. He could not make sound judgements within his own competencies as chief of the intelligence and security sector regarding these incredibly important issues and areas without being fully informed and in full knowledge of what those immediate superiors were doing. And again, Tolimir was answerable to Mladic for the work of men like Beara and Salapura who were immediately subordinate to him. And we will see in July of 1994 -- I beg your pardon, July of 1995 how this operated on the ground. You will also hear that recruitment into the VRS's security intelligence organs was done exclusively with the approval of General Tolimir. General Mladic had the final say, but recruitment into that specialised field - and again we're talking about people that are entrusted with intelligence work, with security work. As I mentioned in the beginning, even the life of General Mladic, his personal protection, it was General Tolimir who had that ultimate authority of who went into those units. Now, the Main Staff, as you can see from this chart there are a lot of names here, but the Main Staff was actually a very small tightly knit group of officers. It really came down to a handful of officers day in and day out who got the job done. And the security organs, you'll learn, were particularly tightly knit for some of the reasons I just mentioned, owing to the nature of their work. You'll hear Colonel Beara refer to General Tolimir not as General, sir, but as Toso. You'll hear that that is General Tolimir's nickname. And Bro. Let's listen to just for a couple of seconds an audio tape. We may have to try to keep the volume a little low. This is an intercepted conversation from the 6th of June, 1995, between General Tolimir and Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the content of the conversation is of no import for our purposes, but what is important is here you see the relationship, Toso, Ljubo, Bro. And you hear General Tolimir giving instructions to General -- to Colonel Beara, go there and then come here and then go take care of that. You'll hear Drina Corps chief of security Vujadin Popovic contacting General Tolimir directly, seeking his assistance about a personal matter. You'll hear security officers referring to each other as Pop and Nedjo, Colonel Beara referring to Drago Nikolic, the chief of security for the Zvornik Brigade, as Drago. Now, let me spend just a couple of minutes focusing on Colonel Salapura. Again I mentioned some of the ways that the intelligence administration obtained its intelligence, and again it provided expert direction, as we call it, to the subordinate units. If there were an intelligence issue that came up, a problem that came in the brigades through the corps, it would be Colonel Salapura that would have to deal with it, with General Tolimir overseeing, obviously. Now, you will hear testimony that Colonel Salapura also professionally managed the 10th Sabotage Detachment which was a special mission unit that was directly involved in executing prisoners in Branjevo on 16 July and at Bisina on the 23rd of July. And they went out and they performed various sabotage missions, attacks, terror attacks. And again by professional management, when we talk about that we mean recommending the most appropriate use of the unit to the actual commander - in this case it would be Mladic - where, when, and how to use a particular unit and ensuring its combat-readiness. So this was a unit within General Tolimir's intelligence administration. So General Tolimir knows what's going on with the 10th Sabotage Detachment, he's responsible for it. And you will see documents showing General Tolimir directly involved in the recruitment process for the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And we talked a little bit about gathering intelligence from prisoners of war. Both the security administration and the intelligence administration under General Tolimir had interests in prisoners of war. And they both had a role to play. I want to show you a document that is a Drina Corps combat-readiness analysis report. We saw one from the Main Staff a while ago from 1993. I'd like to show you one from January of 1995, just to give you an idea of how this actually worked on the ground. I'm throwing out a lot of general descriptions of what these duties were and how they worked, but let's take a look at how it actually worked. Again, Drina Corps command, 28 January 1995, Drina Corps. Under intelligence and security support they talk about -- they've got a role for electronic surveillance, listening in on radio communications by the enemy. So they're using that. And you will hear a lot of evidence about how the Muslim army did the same and some of the most compelling and damning evidence in this case comes from such electronic surveillance that was conducted by both sides. Here the Drina Corps is reporting that the main source of their intelligence data is interrogating POWs and defectors, again, to obtain all this information about the enemy. And the Drina Corps reports that its handling this process very professionally and responsibly with information being presented to the commands and units in whose zone of responsibility the work is being conducted. And most importantly for our purposes, all this intelligence is being sent to the sector for the Main Staff, and again sector, that's Main Staff, that's going to be General Tolimir's sector, where it's professionally processed and then sent back out to the commands in a useful form. That's part of General Tolimir's job. And we'll see when we get into July of 1995 that questions have to be asked within the security administration -- security intelligence administration by General Tolimir himself when all these prisoners are being taken. What's happening to them? Because they present such a potential wealth of intelligence opportunities, among other reasons. And as I mentioned before, it was the military police under the security administration who handled the escort and guarding of POWs. And again, this isn't just guide-lines in a book. As we see from another Drina Corps command document issued in April of 1995, this one from Vujadin Popovic, who you will hear a lot about, the Drina Corps command security chief. In April he's complaining that they're receiving information that POWs are not being handled properly as they're being taken up to a prison camp called Batkovic, and you'll hear about Batkovic later. And what he specifically complains about is these POWs are being taken through sensitive areas, they're not being secured properly. So he orders that their hands must be tied and they must be blindfolded. Fair enough. You don't want to reveal your troops' positions, you don't people to be able to escape. The point is that this is being communicated, this information about how to handle POWs, by General Tolimir. And we have an excerpt here from June of 1995. Again, he's at a National Assembly session. There's been a complaint raised about a particular politician who had been arrested, and General Tolimir specifically cites that directive that came out of his sector. The point is it's his job to know. He is on top of all these issues all the time and has been since the documents you saw from 1993. And you'll see that it's naturally General Tolimir's sector that issues guide-lines for the interrogation of POWs. And related to this important issue of prisoners of war, you will see documents that demonstrate General Tolimir's responsibility and direction of the work of the RS prisoner exchange commission and the prisoner exchange process. He's the one, you'll see from the documents, that makes these ultimate decisions regarding exchanges. They have these commissions, but the Main Staff through General Tolimir retains ultimate approval authority. And again, this is important because it shows that General Tolimir understood the value of POWs, not only as a source of intelligence but as a key to the release of Serb prisoners who were held in Muslim and Croatian prisons in July 1995. And you'll see that General Tolimir was assisted in this process by Colonel Beara. Now, again we're still in the intelligence administration. Underneath Salapura there were three men that you'll hear a fair amount about. The first is Colonel Radoslav Jankovic. In July 1995 he was dispatched from the Main Staff command post to Bratunac during a VRS attack on Srebrenica. He was there in its immediate aftermath, and you'll see some very important orders and intercepts involving him. And you'll see him on the video of the Hotel Fontana meetings which you've heard about and which you will see in full before too long. The second person to keep in mind is Dragomir Pecanac, who was involved in both security and intelligence matters, and we'll see him passing on information from the field to General Tolimir in July of 1995. And thirdly, you'll see documents from Jovica Karanovic who was based at the Main Staff command post in Crna Rijeka. And you'll be seeing him passing critical information up to General Tolimir when General Tolimir is out in the field in July of 1995. So let's turn to the security administration for a few moments. You've heard a lot already about Colonel Ljubo Beara. Again, his responsibilities were the expert direction of the subordinate security organ commands and units, counter-intelligence, maintain the security of the command posts, draft plans for counter-intelligence, protection of the units, combat support, how to keep the combat plans confidential. And as we've already talked about, the security administration had professional control over the military police units. And this is an important area to understand clearly. The security organs, and specifically the security chiefs who headed those organs, be it at the brigade level or at the corps level - let's just use those as examples - the security chiefs of those organs had professional control over the military police units, if it's a Drina Corps military police unit, the Drina Corps security chief has professional management control over those units. That means he proposes to the actual corps commander - in 1995 in July that would have been General Zivanovic and then General Krstic - proposes to the commander how to use those units. He doesn't actually command those units. The security chief does not have the right of actual command to send those units himself somewhere. He can only propose to the actual commander how to use those units. And he's also responsible for their combat-readiness. And that's similar to how the professional lines worked in the other specialised branches as well. But once the commander, whether it's the corps commander, brigade commander, or General Mladic, made a decision about what the military police were going to do, it was the security chief's responsibility and duty to make sure again that the intent of the order was being carried out properly and fully. And that's what we mean again by this controlling aspect of the security chief's job, the management supervisory role of the security chief. And you'll see, therefore, that Colonel Beara supervised the military police battalion of the Main Staff's 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. That MP battalion had its own commander and was himself commanded by the 65th Protection Regiment's commander, but Beara had professional control over that military police battalion commander. And what that meant frequently on the ground, as you'll see from the testimony, is that for your average MP it was the security chief that for all intents and purposes gave the orders. It was the security chief who that MP considered to be his commanding officer. But in terms of the formation and the way it was supposed to work and did work, they had different responsibilities as commander versus security chief. Now, you'll hear that Beara, like the other chiefs of the departments here that you see at the Main Staff, would attend the daily meetings that we'll talk about in a while of the Main Staff, collegiums as they were called. Beara would obtain information from those meetings and he would obtain information from the field. You'll hear testimony from Dutch peacekeepers that Beara was seeking information in 1995 about what the Muslim army was doing, about what Naser Oric was doing, about army positions that the Muslims had. So he was an important conduit of information flowing directly to General Tolimir, and he would remain so in July of 1995. Now, let's go to another document. This is from October of 1994, and the Main Staff is issuing instructions on how this is supposed to work. Specifically, you can see that there is an 80 per cent/20 per cent split that the Main Staff is directing for intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks versus administrative military police and criminal legal tasks. And here in a nutshell we have what I've been talking about, a description of how this professional chain of command relates to the commander's right of command. Security intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit. But with regard to professional activities they are controlled centrally by the security intelligence organs. Here we have it. You can see it in these instructions. "Security intelligence organs at all levels must submit to their superior organ in the professional sense," that means up this professional lines, "... reports ..." And you'll see how important the reporting comes. In the Main Staff -- let me just do a little defining here. When you see VRS GS with that -- what we call a little banana on top, that's VRS Glavni Stab meaning Main Staff. So VRS GS means, in short, the Main Staff. And here the instructions lay out that it is the sector of General Tolimir that takes decisions on transfers, appointments, and assignments to special tasks from their field of work. And again, the recruitment, that's according to special criteria and exclusively with the approval of General Tolimir. Now, you'll hear that the VRS adapted most if not all of the rules of conduct and combat rules from the former JNA to its own needs. That's natural because that's what they were raised as soldiers on. And this included significantly training in the Geneva Conventions, the laws of war. And they were studied at all levels. And on your screen we've got the regulations specifically on the application of international laws of war for the SFRY. This is from 1988. And under the heading "Prevention of Violations of the International Laws of War and Criminal Responsibility for War Crimes," there's a general admonition that everyone is responsible for these kinds of violations. Everybody will be accountable and ignorance basically is no excuse. Okay. Back in 1988 these professionally trained officers also understood that they could be held criminally liable before national courts or before an international court. And it specifically provides that a person organising, inciting, or assisting in the commission of a violation of the laws of war or an accomplice in the same shall also about held responsible as a perpetrator. And that an officer shall be answerable as an accomplice or instigator if he fails to take action against his subordinates who violates the laws of war, he contributes to the repeated commission of such acts by units or individuals subordinated to him. Talking about failure to take action contributing to the repeated commission by units subordinated to him. Now, you'll see that the day after that May 12th, 1992, National Assembly session where President Karadzic issued the Strategic Objectives, the day after President Karadzic signed an order on the application of the rules of international law of war to the VRS. And by another order in August, he made them an explicit part of the duties of VRS members in the service regulations of the army, and that was issued down the chain of command within the army from the Main Staff. So here he we have in October of 1992 from the Main Staff military prosecutor's office these guide-lines. The print is kind of small, so I apologise. But in 1992 this is going out from the Main Staff. "Crimes against humanity and international law can be committed by individuals ... but by their nature these criminal offences are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circles." And it goes on to say: " ... which means that they are committed within the context of broad military operations and on orders from superior officers." Again, recognises those former soldiers doing the shooting at the execution sites you'll hear about don't just wake up one morning and decide to go out and do what they did in July of 1995. The next slide, it just catalogues the various offences, among them starvation of the population, murder, causing great suffering or injury to body or health, forcible relocation. And here is the recognition that the officer class bears particular responsibility. From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders in command of the armed forces. "This responsibility belongs by its nature particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military, or public organisations. "If officers merely found out that units of the armed forces of the Army ... or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures ... this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences." Now, another part of the professional training also required that officers assumed responsibility for documents that went out and reports that went out under their name. Before an officer signed his name to a report, he was expected to have read it, familiarised himself with the contents, and determined it to be valid and in good order. And by signing it he indicates his approval of its contents and he has thereby assumed responsibility for it. This was a principle carried throughout the officer class. And once its passed from its subordinate to the superior up the chain of command, responsibility for that document would lie both with the original author but for the person that gets it next. Now, I already spoke about reporting. The reporting in the VRS was vital for the Main Staff. The superior commands had to be kept informed of what was happening, and timely and accurate reporting was critical so that the commander at whatever level could make the accurate decisions, whether he had to change his decision, modify a decision, or stay put. And the reporting also helped a commander verify that his prior commands were actually being carried out. So they served a number of purposes. And you'll hear that the reporting was done according to a regular schedule, and it had to be otherwise there would have been no way to control the process. The lower-level commands had to send their reports up at a certain time so their superior commands could review everything, create their own reports to send them up to the next level of command. So you had battalion, brigades, corps, all compiling their own records after receiving reports from their subordinate commands, analysing them, processing them, and sending them up so that they could be used by the superior command. General Mladic would speak with the corps commanders each day by telephone often. He had to do that later in the evening because oftentimes the situation on the field had changed between the time a report went up to a particular level and made it to the Main Staff or had been processed in the Main Staff. And then all of those reports would be put together at the Main Staff, culled, analysed and put together in a report that went to President Karadzic as I mentioned before. These reports were a vital link between the Main Staff and President Karadzic. They informed him of what was developing, what was important, so he could make decisions as supreme commander of the armed forces. And in addition to this type of reporting, again you also had the reporting that was going up the professional lines of command as we already talked. So you've got two types of reporting that are always going on, always communications going on every day. It was in some ways the life blood of how the army worked. And related to that is the issue of communications. You can't report if you don't have good comms from the field, if you're reporting back to your brigade, if you can't communicate from the brigade to the corps, you're going to be in trouble. So you'll see the efforts that the Main Staff made to ensure that it maintained constant communications with subordinate units, especially because General Mladic would be out in the field, he would send his main assistant commanders out in the field. And you'll see that they were able to maintain these communications by setting up forward command posts. And you'll see the initials IKM over and over again in this case. IKM means forward command post. They would set up IKMs where you would have an officer forward with its own communications equipment. Or sometimes they would utilise the communications equipment of the local brigade or corps. But they always stayed in contact. General Milovanovic will tell you even when he was in the Krajina he was able to speak with General Mladic on an encrypted line, and he was able to contact the Main Staff every day. And you will see during the Srebrenica and Zepa operations General Tolimir communicating with the Main Staff and subordinate units and officers from a variety of locations. You will see General Tolimir issuing proposals, orders, reports, from the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica, from the Rogatica command, from the Drina Corps forward command post in a place called Krivace. You'll see him do it from another forward command post called Borike in a little school in a village near Zepa, near Rogatica. Everywhere he goes, he makes sure he's got good communications, communications officer and equipment. If he doesn't have it, he'll find some way to get it. So as we go and look at these documents you'll see at the top of the document where it's coming from, Drina Corps IKM Krivace. Drina Corps IKM Pribicevac. General Tolimir would not have been able to do his job without being able to maintain these good communications. I just want to again look at the words of General Tolimir describing how the Main Staff in fact operated. Again, this was a contentious meeting at the National Assembly. The army was coming in for some heat for what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa, and more importantly what was happening at that time with the collapse of the VRS defences in the west. But here you'll see General Tolimir responding to a criticism and he says, Hey, we're the smallest Main Staff in the world - again you see this GS with the banana on the top - General Miletic is currently in the Main Staff and it was always so. General Miletic is the operations man. He is the one that stays home to receive all that information and get the information out. General Milosevic, that refers to Dragomir Milosevic, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander, will not be left alone. We are always sending someone from the Main Staff and we are still doing it. There is a forward command post that is stronger than his is and is located in that part of the Sarajevo front. There are two forward command posts of the Main Staff in his zone. Again, this practice of the Main Staff sending its representatives forward. We have been keeping General Milovanovic as the most experienced commanding officer as well as General Mladic, and he misspoke, he meant General Maric, out at this front, this Grahovo-Glamoc front that was collapsing. And winds up saying and summing: We make expert analyses, we prepare directives, and based on those directives we all go in the field and work in accordance with the assignments that we received." That's it in a nutshell. Mladic gave these Main Staff officers these critical tasks because they were his most trusted and experienced officers. And by virtue of the fact that as general officers, that means at the rank of general, they were expected to and did possess the necessary skills regardless of whatever their professional line of expertise was. And you'll see that when General Mladic left the command post in Crna Rijeka he would leave one of his most trusted officers in charge if they weren't already out in the field. And you'll see an intercept where General Mladic tells General Tolimir, "You're taking over completely for me there in command." Before we started looking at the Main Staff structure and operation, we had left off with this combat order to attack Zepa and the Gorazde enclaves and its provisions for moving out the Muslims from those enclaves. And again as I mentioned, the UN issued another resolution making Zepa a safe area. And you'll see that as part of this safe area regime the warring parties were supposed to demilitarise. They signed agreements, pledged to remove all their weapons and hand in their weapons and store them in weapons collection points at various places. And I think one thing we can all agree on, Your Honours, is that the enclaves were never demilitarised. That is not contested by the Prosecution. They were not demilitarised. Some small arms, broken weapons were turned in. But a lot of them weren't, and you'll hear that the Muslim forces were reinforced throughout this period from 1993 all the way to 1995 by air-drops of weapons so that they were able to conduct military strikes outwards from the enclaves, primarily to tie-down Serb forces, draw them away from other areas, keep them stuck to the enclaves, distract them from the Sarajevo front. And you'll see that this created a situation for the VRS that became increasingly problematic. It couldn't afford the manpower and resources to constantly surround and enclose these enclaves where these hit-and-run sabotage attacks were being committed by the Muslim forces operating in violation of the agreements. Let's just take a look at a map which shows the enclave of Srebrenica and how the peacekeeping scheme worked in 1995. You'll hear that there was a battalion of Dutch soldiers who were stationed there. We refer to them as DutchBat for short. They were actually the third rotation, so this -- you'll see sometimes referred to as DutchBat 3. They were based in two compounds. One right next to where it says "Srebrenica" basically, in Srebrenica town they had a base, and the other up in the village of Potocari, which you'll see if you follow that's a road that's running north to south between Potocari and Srebrenica. So they had two compounds, Bravo compound in the south and Charlie compound to the north between Srebrenica and Bratunac. And the way it was supposed to work was the United Nations set up observation posts encircling the enclave. We refer to them as OPs, and you can see them marked there starting from the west, Alpha, and so forth, Mike, Oscar, and Papa, right near the base in Potocari. One OP that will be particularly important for us to pay attention to is all the way down in the south-east corner you'll see an E denoting OP Echo. And that will be a source of dispute, you'll hear, and ultimately you'll hear that it was blasted out by the Serbs as a prelude to their attack on Srebrenica in July of 1995. The OPs were brightly lit, painted white. They were made to be visible. They weren't meant to be surreptitious observation posts. They were supposed to scream, We are the UN, we are here, and we are watching. They were supposed to be watching to make sure that both parties laid down their weapons, but you will hear for a variety of reasons - there's fault to be laid at many feet - they weren't able to do that job. You'll hear that in Zepa the peacekeepers were Ukrainians, about 80 of them in July of 1995. I just want to while we're on this map show you -- point out this very significant road that runs east-west between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. If you see Bratunac on the right, the top-most marking there, that's a road that runs through Glogova, Kravica, Sandici, then to Konjevic Polje, and it intersects at that point with the road that runs north-south from Milici, if you see that down there, to the west, through Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and then up north ultimately to Zvornik. You'll hear a lot about this road in July of 1995. Basically what happened was the areas were supposed to be demilitarised, they weren't. There were tit-for-tat attacks. General Tolimir would complain in his intelligence reports that they were happening, and it was true. And in July 1994 after about a year of this, we'll see that in connection with a six-month combat-readiness analysis, General Mladic tours the corps and he meets at the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica with the brigade commanders. And he's briefed by the Drina Corps and brigade commanders. And two days later, two after this briefing on -- in early, early July, I think July 1, in fact, we see the Bratunac Brigade commander. At that time it was Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic. On 4 July 1994 he issues a report to his brigade. And you can see on this document that this is being distributed all the way to the 3rd Infantry Battalion, so it's going down so that all the soldiers in the trenches are hearing the message in this report. What does he say? He says: "We have won the war in Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal - an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily." Okay. Sounds like maybe he's talking about straight warfare, crushing the enemy's troops. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." Okay. Well, maybe he's talking about the soldiers again. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive here." En masse. He's talking about the civilian population which has been the target, as you've seen, going all the way back to Directive 4. And when the commander who you will hear personifies command, that is, sets the example for his subordinates and makes a statement like this that is distributed down to the battalion levels, of course they get the message. And what's important, Your Honours, is that Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic isn't making this stuff up himself. He is passing down to his command what he understands are the objectives of his superior command which he had just met with. And you'll hear that two days later at an Assembly session -- I apologise -- about two weeks later at an Assembly session, President Karadzic in Pale has this to say about the strategic goals in case there were any doubt that they are still viewed as being unfulfilled, uncompleted. He said that the primary strategic aim was to get rid of the enemies in our house, the Croats and the Muslims, and not to be in the same state with them anymore. And so what we see being issued by the Main Staff three days after that speech by President Karadzic is an order. The first item is General Mladic is saying basically the peace agreement setting up the safe areas and the UN peacekeepers, that's all null and void because of the attacks that had been happening. So he says he wants to -- he orders the communication and departure of Muslims from the enclaves at all costs. By "communication," he means the frequent travel between Srebrenica and Zepa that has historically occurred looking for food, running goods, weapons. So he orders that this transport be tightened up and that the Main Staff is going to take further control over this. No equipment is to be allowed into the enclaves, apart from food and medication which are approved by the Main Staff. They're going to have control over this process. "In the orders they issue, corps commands shall regulate check-points ... thoroughly check all cargo authorised by the ... Main Staff ..." And you will hear about how the Main Staff implemented the strict control over the movement of convoys in connection with the document called Directive 7 you've probably already heard about, and we'll get to that in a little bit. But here we have in 1994 the Main Staff already setting up the mechanism. He wants the enclaves to be fully mined, surrounded. He wants the Muslims not to be able to leave the enclaves. You might be asking yourself, "Well, I thought the whole point was to get them to leave the enclaves," but what he's talking about here is he wants to close them in, pen them in. Don't let them get out, don't let them get weapons to each other, pen them in. That's what's going on here. And then he instructs that the corps and brigade commands shall start basically ramping up their sniping. And then in paragraph 13 he says basically because the Muslims have thrown out the agreement by their sabotage attacks, I want you to take measures to reduce the enclaves to a particular area, geographic area. Now, this reference to reducing the enclaves, the evidence will show - and it's the Prosecution's position - is not the same as what happens in March of 1995 with the issuance of Directive 7. What we have here in 1994 is the Main Staff keeping its eyes on this strategically important area and beginning to turn up the heat. They're not bringing it up to the boiling point yet, but the Main Staff is turning up the heat. And you'll see what happens with its policy of sniping, you'll hear evidence about how the sniping did get ramped up, how civilians were sniped and killed. And I won't show it to you now but you will see being the well-organised disciplined army that the VRS was, General Zivanovic, the Drina Corps commander, adopting General Mladic's order virtually word for word, just putting his name at the end. So we see from 1992 to 1993 to 1994 the Main Staff always, always has its eyes on the enclaves. And as we enter 1995, we'll see that the parties have entered a cessation of hostilities agreement and that in connection with that agreement there have been what are called joint commissions formed, where the warring parties are supposed to get together and monitor this cessation of hostilities agreement. And this agreement entailed a number of issues which were of importance to General Tolimir's sector, and you will see General Tolimir personally involved in them. And what we'll see, for example, is Main Staff document 7 January 1995. General Tolimir had been attending these meetings. He was actually a signatory to a freedom of movement agreement. He's meeting at the highest levels with UNPROFOR, he's representing the army. And he's keeping President Karadzic abreast of what is going on because these issues directly implicate the enclaves. We'll see number 2. He is telling the corps commands that they are to submit to the Main Staff proposed locations for UNPROFOR observation stations along the lines of disengagement, to see whether they're going to monitor the cease-fire. Now, this isn't General Tolimir issuing a combat order, he's not acting as a commander here. But he is issuing instructions in line certainly with the intention of General Mladic. He is telling the corps commands: You are to submit. And you can rest assured that if General Tolimir writes "you are to submit" they will submit, because they know that he is writing that with the authority of General Mladic. Related to the cessation of hostilities agreement you will see again General Tolimir in February sending out to the corps this notification. He's saying look, we've looked at the maps you sent us where you were supposed to mark the lines of confrontation between the VRS and the Muslim forces. And he's saying: Drina Corps, you did a terrible job, you did a sloppy job. You didn't even demarcate certain areas along the line. And he's talking specifically about Srebrenica. And then he points out: And look, it's not clear who is in control of this Zeleni Jadar factory near this check-point. And what he's referring to there is this OP Echo that I mentioned a few moments ago when we were looking at the map at the south-east corner of the enclave. That observation post is located on a critical east-west asphalt road, and it was critical if the Serbs were going to launch an attack on Srebrenica to have that road and that location secured, and he's talking about that particular area here in February of 1995. It's his job to be on top of this type of intelligence information, and you will see how that plays into his actions in July. And then he gives again instructions: "When going to the field you are to justify all of the disputed issues ..." And then he basically throws the maps back at them and says: Do it right. About a month later we see another document from General Tolimir, March of 1995, March 19th entitled: "Establishment of a security system and control of the territory." What's going on is if you remember that map we looked at a little while ago, that key road from Bratunac that ran east-west to Konjevic Polje and that intersection between the east-west and north-south roads, he's talking about an area basically at that intersection, an area of Konjevic Polje, and he's saying in this communication: We've got unoccupied areas that Muslim forces are going to move into if we don't do something about it. And he sends this to President Karadzic and he proposes to President Karadzic that MUP units, Ministry of the Interior units, get dispatched there. And he talks about both of these roads, the importance of this area to the east-west road and the north-south road, again referring to this area of the Birac and Podrinje. And then he says please inform the Main Staff what the MUP's going to do about it. And you'll see documents, Your Honours, during the trial, that within about 36 hours President Karadzic through his Ministry of the Interior command has made sure that there are MUP police stationed at that intersection. And this intersection will be critical to understand during the events of the murder operation and the forcible transfer. I see it's break time, Mr. President, and this is as good as any for me. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. We must break now and have the second break and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, during this period in February/March of 1995, General Tolimir, you will see, is receiving intelligence and security reports about the situation in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves from his subordinates like Beara, who are in the field meeting with UNPROFOR and going to Zepa to gather information. You will also hear that they are receiving information that - and this is in early 1995 - that Muslims are trying to leave the enclaves because of shortages and poor living conditions. It's been that way for, as you've already heard, from early on in the war, no doubt intensified by General Mladic's order that we saw from July of 1994, sealing off the enclaves from each other, basically penning people in, turning the heat up a little bit, but not to the boiling point yet. General Tolimir receives this information and he passes it up once again to President Karadzic and the various intelligence agencies because this is important information to know about these strategically valuable areas. And he's also receiving intelligence information about the military and political leaders in Srebrenica and Zepa. And one example you'll see, there's a Drina Corps intelligence officer by the name of Golic, and he sends up his reporting, his professional chain of command an intelligence report that talks about Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa leaving the enclaves and lays out the identities of various military -- high-ranking military officers in Zepa, some of the political leaders. So in this document you'll see the same Avdo Palic, who you'll hear is the Muslim army leader, the commander of the Zepa Brigade, Hamdija Torlak, Emir Imamovic, these are civilian leaders of the Muslim community. General Tolimir is receiving information about these individuals, and it's going where it needs to go, up from the corps to the Main Staff and ultimately to General Mladic. And you'll see this document from Major Golic and it's got General Mladic's handwriting on it. There's a note written by General Mladic that: General Tolimir -- Toso, we should process this and distribute it to the 65th Protection Regiment which is in the area. This must be used. You'll see examples of this how of how this intelligence is going to be employed during the events of July 1995. And again, General Tolimir is receiving this information about the humanitarian situation in the enclaves. So when these terrible events begin to unfold in July of 1995, Srebrenica and Zepa aren't just names in a report, places on a map to General Tolimir; these are areas about which he possesses a deep working knowledge, set against the general Strategic Objectives that we've been talking about all day today. It's important to keep that in mind, that he is looking at these enclaves from both perspectives. And heading further into 1995, the evidence will show that the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership was united in its hardening position regarding the eastern enclaves, as both sides began to foresee a decisive engagement or battle on the horizon that would end the war with respect to this area. They saw some kind of definitive military action coming at some point. You will hear from General Rupert Smith who was the commander of the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was based in Sarajevo, and he'll tell you about meetings that he had with President Karadzic, sometimes alone, sometimes in support of other high-ranking UN officials with, among others, President Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and so forth. Sometimes General Tolimir would be there, sometimes General Gvero. But from early 1995 the conditions were already severe in the enclave and UNPROFOR complained about them to the Serb military and political leaders. And you'll see that the VRS had always restricted the inflow of supplies, humanitarian aid to the enclaves even before March of 1995. But you'll see - and we'll look at the document in a minute - that boiling point, finally the gas being turned on to get there. What we're looking at is another directive. This is Directive number 7. We talked about Directive number 4. This is from March of 1995. This is just the cover letter, as it were, distributing it to the corps. It's dated March 17th. And here's the first page. Again, this is the result of the combat-readiness analysis that was conducted earlier in the year in January, all of the highest-level military political leaders get together and decide what the tasks are going to be for the upcoming war -- for the upcoming period of the war. And the Main Staff drafts this directive and issues it in March, and the date of the directive is actually March 8th of 1995. We know General Tolimir is involved in this combat-readiness analysis that spawned Directive 7 and we know that he's involved in the drafting of this document because these are drafted through what we call the full method, where all the assistant commanders contribute their expertise in putting it together as a military document. Now, we'll see that there's a section concerning the main characteristics of the international military and political situation, just as we have in some of the other combat orders where we saw General Tolimir's message being incorporated, his assessments being incorporated, and here we have a very detailed section on the probable objective and plans of the Muslim forces. This again, this is General Tolimir's job. This is his sector's responsibility, knowing what these are going to be to the best of their abilities. And here we are, the assessment that the Muslims are planning a spring offensive, that they're going to focus on linking the enclaves and reaching the Drina River. They're concerned, as we saw in one of President Karadzic's earlier addresses, that the Muslims are going to themselves reach the Drina and create their own what they called the green corridor, transversal Islamic corridor across Bosnia. Now, this information that we see about the assessment of the enemy is clearly reached, made its way into Directive 7, help shape it, steer it. And you'll see in a follow-up directive to this directive an explicit reference to General Tolimir's intelligence reports. This is in the section that we're looking at here devoted to the tasks of the VRS. These are the more general tasks that are being issued, the goals: "While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible preventing even communications between individuals in the two enclaves." Again, splitting apart, sealing off, not necessarily an illegal motive. Of course, what the evidence will show is that all along there has always been an illegal motive pursuant to Directives 1 and 3 -- Strategic Objectives 1 and 3, move the Muslims out. And this section is immediately followed up by this passage which instructs the Drina Corps: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope for further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, let's just look at this for a moment. Really, this is the latest incarnation, if you will, from the language of Directive 4 that we've seen as the common thread all throughout this illegal objective targeting the civilian population of these enclaves. This is an illegal motive to create a situation that is so intolerable, to make life so unbearable with no hope for survival that they are going to leave. It's a clear order to create the conditions to deprive the Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa, of the necessities for survival. And we'll see in just a moment another part that links with this portion of the directive, that loss of hope of survival is going to be tied to the supply of humanitarian aid to the civilian population and re-supply to UNPROFOR to weaken UNPROFOR. So we have this section here that talks about creating this unbearable situation, no survival for life. The next section talks about another operation in case UNPROFOR leaves, where they will definitively liberate the Drina Valley region. And here we have the section I was just talking about. "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations ..." The evidence will be crystal clear that the relevant military organisations responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations is the Main Staff. " ... through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Now, let's unpack this little bit. There's a lot in this section. Again, the evidence will be clear that it's the Main Staff that decides what convoys get to go in or not, whether it's for UNPROFOR, for the peacekeepers, or whether it's UNHCR, food, sanitary supplies for the Muslim population in Srebrenica and Zepa. This is talking about the Main Staff and the state military -- the state organ you'll hear is a commission that in the end had to defer to the Main Staff. " ... through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits ..." "Unobtrusively," Your Honours, they're being careful here, they're being smart. The evidence will show that General Tolimir, like General Gvero, always had his eye on the international community, on international opinion. He and General Gvero next to General Mladic were the most public faces of the VRS, interviewed on the news, making the appearances before the National Assembly. It was General Tolimir's job to have that wide field perspective I mentioned before of what was going on in the larger international community, the larger military field of vision, and on the ground as well. That's why they're being smart and they're being careful. They're saying let's do it, let's do it unobtrusively, we'll make them dependent on us and we're going to do it in such a way that we don't trigger UN intervention or international intervention like there was in 1993 when General Morillon came. And you'll hear this theme over and over again. We can't let ourselves be stopped like we were in 1993 when Morillon came in and put those peacekeepers around Srebrenica. So this is a clear order to create the conditions in combination with that earlier section, with that appalling language about making life so unbearable, that the Main Staff sends out to its subordinate commands to implement on the ground. And I'll save a little bit of time I hope and we'll see it some other time, but you will see this language about making life unbearable being repeated word for word by General Zivanovic in his order to the Drina Corps, to whom this is going to, to implement the policy on the ground. Again, these are not just words. These are orders to do things, to create these conditions, and they are taking -- they are taken deadly seriously because they know how this system works in the army. Orders are given, they're meant to be followed, they shall be reported on back up the chain; and if they're not, somebody's going to be held accountable for it. So you'll see General Zivanovic sends that language out: Create these conditions that are so unbearable that we will force them to leave. And this, Your Honours, is where we see the forcible transfer operation starting to the brought to the boil. You'll see sniping, shelling, and the slow steady strangling of these enclaves all throughout the spring of 1995. The Main Staff deliberately restricted these supplies both to DutchBat as well as to the civilian population of Srebrenica and Zepa. This was part of this common plan and organised effort to remove these populations. Let's start with the convoy restrictions. I'm going tell you a little bit about how that worked. It was actually very simple. If UNPROFOR needed supplies, Your Honours, or to rotate its peacekeepers or military observers, they would send a fax over to the Main Staff. There was a colonel there by the name of Djurdjic who was the point person for these requests, but Mladic relied on his top men like General Tolimir, General Gvero, working together to review these requests, make proposals to him. And with respect to the humanitarian aid convoys, as I mentioned there was a so-called RS commission for -- it was a state committee for co-operation with international organisations, humanitarian organisations. The Main Staff had a representative on that committee, and you'll see convoy request after convoy request where the Main Staff says, "We have reviewed the committee's plan. We approve this and this and this, but we deny this and this and this." So it's, as you will see, the Main Staff that ultimately retained the power over what was going into the enclaves and what was not. And you'll see examples of these requests with General Mladic's handwritten notes to Toso, Gvero, your input and opinion, your advice, your proposals. And you'll see, you'll get familiar with General Tolimir's signature and his initials. Sometimes you'll even see General Tolimir's comments written right next to the fax or written right on the fax request. Let me just give you a little sense of what some of these convoy denials were like and how they operated. You'll see a notification signed by General Miletic from March saying that we reduced the plan for the enclaves in number of vehicles and the transport of fuel is not permitted. Despite the information on restrictions, we submitted to the co-ordinating body, we expect that UNHCR will try to bring fuel into the enclaves which has to be prevented. In another convoy denial from March you'll see the following being prevented from going into Srebrenica: Diesel, dry rations, frozen and cold food, water trailer, spare parts. And there's a note. Instructions in the last paragraph: Give information on the convoys that were not approved to check-points and do not relate them to third persons or give any explanation to UNPROFOR representatives, as if you did not receive it. If a convoy appears at a crossing return it to the place of origin. Field beds, hospital beds. From UNHCR a request for convoys was approved by the state committee, and this is from April of 1995, but the VRS denied beef, salt, oil, clavers [phoen] for Srebrenica. This was on the 8th, et 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, and 13th of April, 1995. That material and those supplies were supposed to go in. School supplies denied. You'll see the examples yourselves during trial. I won't take up any more time going through them. Let me just give you one more example that sort of exemplifies the problems that this caused for the UN that was charged with getting this humanitarian aid into the enclaves. This is how it affected by June the UN: "Problems with convoys, both logistics re-supply," that's DutchBat, "and UNHCR," that's the civilians, "continue in many parts of the UNPROFOR AOR," area of responsibility. "The 56 truck convoy bound for the eastern enclaves arrived in Belgrade yesterday. However, the BSA ..." and you'll see that UNPROFOR referred to the VRS as the BSA in a lot of their documents, the Bosnian Serb army, so if you see BSA it's the same thing as VRS. "The BSA has cut the number of trucks from 56 to 23, has cut the amount of food by 50 per cent, and the amount of fuel by 70 per cent, has rejected the passage of two ambulances needed for UN troops, and has insisted that those personnel travelling with the convoy to the enclaves must also depart with it. Though no one else may, in other words, preventing any troop rotation or reinforcement." Another element of this policy to unobtrusively restrict the permits was to prevent the rotation of UN personnel. They'd let people out but they wouldn't let fresh peacekeepers come back in. So you had an increasingly undersupplied, underfed, underarmed group of peacekeepers in Srebrenica and Zepa that was dwindling in number. So that by July of 1995 you will see just how operationally impaired they were by the time the attack came. Now, when the Main Staff did approve a convoy - and they did approve convoys, they didn't pull the plug completely because they knew that they could only go so far. You'll see over and over again. The evidence in this case will show that General Tolimir, General Gvero, Main Staff knew just how for they could go before triggering international condemnation and action. And it was the action that they were worried about, specifically the deployment of NATO air power in support of the UNPROFOR troops or the insertion of ground forces in support. Now, when the Main Staff did approve a convoy, they had to be checked in Zvornik, depending on which bridge they came over. And you'll see reports from the Zvornik Brigade up to the corps detailing what they have removed from the convoys. Because they know what's approved by the Main Staff and what's not. You'll see, for example, a field steriliser, a veld steriliser that's taken out. That's a medical device. You'll see at one point laundry detergent, cleaning stuff, cleaning fluids, shampoo, towels, all being removed. And General Tolimir was part of this whole process for a number of reasons, one of which was it was the military police units and the security organs which were responsible for the operation of these check-points. You'll see many examples of these convoy notification documents with the words handwritten "security, security organ," or the name of the actual security officer for the brigade written on it, indicating that these requests are going to the security organ. And when the approvals came through you will see that it was the security branch's job to monitor and to enforce this VRS policy of who and what was coming into the enclaves, and there's naturally an intelligence aspect to that. So that's another reason why General Tolimir is responsible for this activity in addition to the illegal motive that's always, always present. But on the ground, on the ground in the Srebrenica enclave for the DutchBat peacekeepers, for the suffering civilians in Srebrenica, the Main Staff convoy procedure became embodied in Momir Nikolic, who you will hear was the security and intelligence assistant commander for the Bratunac Brigade. Because the final check-point for these convoys before entering Srebrenica was in Bratunac at a check-point referred to as Yellow Bridge, near a Dutch observation post Papa. The convoys would be stopped and rigorously checked by Momir Nikolic, and you will see again documents, some with his handwriting on it, one that says "not a single convoy or ICRC team or MSF may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence." And again, just like Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic in July of 1994 isn't just making up this stuff about having to force the Muslims out make life unbearable, Momir Nikolic is receiving his instructions from his superior command. And the Main Staff was well familiar with Momir Nikolic, and you'll see Main Staff documents mentioning Nikolic by name, which they say: "We set out the manner of inspection and requests in this connection." Let's look at another document. Again, this is a document created in connection with a combat-readiness analysis. This one is a sixth-month combat-readiness analysis. You might be getting a sense of how organised and disciplined the VRS was. A brigade putting this report together element by element and under "intelligence-security support," the report writes: "During 1995, international organisations, and their representatives have passed through and stayed temporarily in the brigade's area of responsibility." And it goes on to say that they were monitored and every single event was reported to the superior organs and the Main Staff. And then it refers to the check-point for the control of all international organisations, and, again, functioning in accordance with the orders of the Main Staff and instructions of the brigade commander. Now, you'll hear how the conditions worsened and worsened from March 1995 until the attack in July. And this unobtrusive issuing of permits by the VRS didn't have to be so severe to create corresponding misery on the ground in Srebrenica because the conditions were already so bad. It didn't take a whole lot of denied convoys to make the people even more hungrier or more miserable or without even the dwindling medical supplies they needed in the enclave. So the corresponding effect was magnified because of the conditions that already prevailed. Added to that you'll hear evidence that the sniping increased during this period of time. And you remember that order about the snipers and the silencers, it was the Main Staff that ran the sniper school, and of course it's the Bratunac Brigade soldiers who were shooting these Muslim civilians. You'll hear about that. That order went out at the same time basically that the Bratunac Brigade commander was talking about making life unbearable for the Muslims, and the sniping got worse and worse and so did the shelling. You'll hear testimony from survivors, witnesses about the intensified shelling during 1995. And you'll see, as we did in 1993, intelligence and security reports from General Tolimir describing this shelling as part of a propaganda campaign, disinformation. And you'll hear about a notorious example of the VRS shelling of civilians that took place on the 25th of May, 1995. On that day in retaliation for NATO air-strikes on an ammo dump in Pale you will hear evidence that the VRS shelled all of the safe areas that day. And you'll hear that in Tuzla over 70 civilians, most of them youngsters, celebrating Tito's birthday were killed when they were celebrating outdoors in the early, the early evening, in the old town. They were killed by massive and deliberate VRS shelling. And you'll hear that almost simultaneously the VRS shelled Srebrenica killing a 9-year-old girl and seriously wounding her sister, and you'll have testimony from that sister who survived. The evidence will show that this was a co-ordinated attack on the civilian population for no other reason than to inflict terror and suffering. And you'll hear from witnesses as well about an attack on the 24th of June, 1995, you'll hear from a UN military observer. You'll see reports that the VRS inserted the 10th Sabotage Unit, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, to fire on civilian targets in Srebrenica, and that resulted in deaths of civilians as well. Momir Nikolic, the Bratunac Brigade security and intelligence assistant commander will tell you that General Tolimir's direct subordinate, Colonel Salapura, who we talked about earlier, directed that action on the ground. So by late June -- and here we have just one example of many protest letters from the UN. General Smith is protesting to General Mladic that on almost a daily basis he's receiving reports of shelling of populated areas, Bihac safe area, Srebrenica safe area, Gorazde, and Sarajevo, safe areas. And again General Tolimir has his spin ready. After this June 24th sabotage attack where civilians are killed in that terror attack, General Tolimir writes: "In the area of Srebrenica there is increased distrust among the population in relation to the military and civilian leadership, and also accusations that they have caused the reprisal of the VRS by the infiltration and action of sabotage and terrorist groups in Serbian territory. The 28th Division command is circulating disinformation that the VRS carried out a sabotage attack on civilian features, wanting to cause condemnation by the international community." Again, this is the message that General Tolimir has been shaping and steering since day one. The MO never changed. You'll hear soon enough about the effects that these restrictions had on the DutchBat peacekeepers and on the civilian population. You'll hear about the meetings that the UN leadership had with the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership, the concerns that were expressed. You'll hear President Karadzic repeating the assessment of General Tolimir that they were expecting the Muslims to try to break out of the enclaves and President Karadzic describing the enclaves as a time bomb about to explode. By July of 1995 the UN peacekeepers who were supposed to number 600 were down to 350. They hadn't been permitted to bring in weapons. They had to use the weapons that were used by the prior DutchBat rotations. They weren't allowed to bring in fresh ammunition. They weren't allowed to bring in testing equipment for their anti-tank and other weapons systems. They hadn't been allowed to bring in fuel since February. They were cooking on wood. They had to conduct foot patrols instead of APC patrols so they could not enforce their mandate in that respect. They were living on dried rations because they had no fresh food. Because of the lack of fuel they had to use candle light at night. They didn't have electricity to purify water. And for the civilians in Srebrenica the situation was devastating. UNPROFOR could not support the medical facilities with its medical supplies. People were starving. People were getting killed as they tried to leave Srebrenica for Zepa in search of food. What we're looking at, Your Honours, is a photograph that was taken by a DutchBat officer. These are civilians from Srebrenica gathered around a garbage truck searching for food. And you'll hear that they regularly did this, going through the dumped garbage looking for anything edible. General Tolimir knew what the conditions were like even before Directive 7 began its operation. Again, this is even before this unobtrusive issuing of permits was underway. So you can imagine what the conditions were like, maybe you can't. I don't think I can really imagine what it was like by July of 1995. You'll hear a DutchBat officer, the deputy commander of the battalion in Srebrenica, Colonel Franken refer to it as convoy terror and that's what it was. Directive 7 was implemented efficiently and brutally, and you'll see the effect it had on DutchBat's ability to respond to the military attack that was coming. Now, I see we're at the end of the day and I've actually found myself at the beginning of a new chapter, so I'll pick up there tomorrow, Mr. President -- Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Not tomorrow, of course not. We will adjourn now, but I think we should discuss on Monday at the end of the session the question in which way we should schedule our days, with breaks and the duration of the sessions. We adjourn now and we'll resume next Monday, 9.00, in this courtroom.
